stem:
A 22-year-old man of African descent presents to the emergency department with severe bone pain in both thighs after a short viral illness. He has a childhood history of recurrent painful crises and intermittent jaundice. Examination shows tenderness over several long bones without overlying cellulitis.

Which mechanism most directly explains tissue ischemia during these episodes?

options.label: A
options.text: Abnormally shaped cells lodge in narrow capillaries
options.misconception: None; sickled cells lodge in capillaries and block flow.
options.explanation: Sickled erythrocytes cannot fold to squeeze through narrow capillaries, lodging there and blocking blood flow to tissues.

options.label: B
options.text: Autoantibodies lyse erythrocytes in the spleen only
options.misconception: Immune hemolysis is being substituted for vaso-occlusion.
options.explanation: Autoimmune hemolysis is a different pathway; sickle ischemia follows capillary lodging of deformed cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Marrow fibrosis replaces normal erythropoiesis entirely
options.misconception: Myelofibrosis is being confused with hemoglobin S vasculopathy.
options.explanation: Marrow fibrosis does not explain acute vaso-occlusive bone pain from capillary obstruction.

options.label: D
options.text: Platelet plugs occlude arteries without shape change
options.misconception: Primary thrombosis is being confused with sickled-cell lodging.
options.explanation: The grounded mechanism is deformed erythrocytes lodging in capillaries, not isolated platelet arterial plugs.

options.label: E
options.text: Cholesterol emboli shower distal arterioles after plaques
options.misconception: Atherosclerotic embolization is being inferred in a young adult.
options.explanation: Cholesterol emboli are unrelated to hemoglobin S–driven erythrocyte deformation and capillary lodging.

context: Learning objective: infer capillary lodging of sickled cells as the ischemia mechanism.
